title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Memory — August 2026

studies.title: Semaglutide is linked to fewer cognitive complaints in people with psychiatric illness
studies.ns_score_reason: very large cohort and a topical drug, but strictly observational and based on clinician-recorded signs rather than cognitive testing.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Using de-identified US electronic health records (NeuroBlu, 1999–2024), researchers compared 13,007 adults with a psychiatric diagnosis who started an antidiabetic drug (mean age 62; 1261 started semaglutide). Over 12 months, clinician-rated cognitive signs/symptoms — covering memory, attention and orientation — were lower with semaglutide than with no antidiabetic treatment (mean ratio 0.75), glipizide or empagliflozin, with the strongest signal in memory and in people with major depression.
studies.why_it_matters: Cognitive fog in depression and psychosis is common, disabling and essentially untreated; this raises the possibility that a widely prescribed GLP-1 drug touches it, though only a randomised trial could show causation.
studies.pitch_angle: "The weight-loss drug that may also clear the fog." Open on a patient with depression whose main complaint is not low mood but forgetting names and losing threads mid-sentence. Call Maxime Taquet or Riccardo De Giorgi at Oxford, who have a track record of large EHR emulations, and ask them directly what the confounding-by-indication problem is here.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-policy or business outlet: GLP-1 agonists are accumulating off-label cognitive and psychiatric signals faster than trials can test them, and health systems are now the de facto evidence generators through EHR mining — a piece about who owns and profits from that evidence pipeline (note Holmusk's involvement).
studies.caveats: Observational, cannot establish causation; outcome is a composite of routine clinician-recorded signs, not standardised neuropsychological testing; two co-authors are employed by and hold equity in the data company (Holmusk/KKT Technologies), one author has consultancy fees from Holmusk; unmeasured confounding by weight loss, glycaemic control and prescribing preference is likely.

studies.title: Sleep sharpens memory for who told you what — and makes conversation more efficient
studies.ns_score_reason: extends the well-known sleep-consolidation effect into genuinely social territory across three experiments, but the mechanism hunt came up empty.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Across three experiments, participants did a matcher-director communication task (on computer, then face-to-face) with two partners before and after 12 hours of sleep or wake. Sleepers showed better item recognition *and* better source memory — who said what — and used fewer words to describe previously discussed items, though this efficiency was not partner-specific. A third experiment with a polysomnographically recorded two-hour nap found no relationship between slow oscillation–spindle coupling and retention.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests sleep does not just file away facts but preserves the shared conversational history that makes talking to a familiar person efficient — a social function of sleep that has barely been studied.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why a bad night's sleep makes you a worse conversationalist." Open on the awkward moment of re-explaining something you already agreed on last week. Lead with the source-memory result — sleep protects *who* said it, not just *what*. Call Heather Ferguson at Kent or Gareth Gaskell at York; press Gaskell on why the spindle analysis was null.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest magazine on "common ground" as the invisible infrastructure of relationships — how couples, colleagues and old friends build a compressed private language, and what happens to it in insomnia, shift work and dementia.
studies.caveats: Sleep-versus-wake designs confound time of day and circadian phase; the nap experiment was null on electrophysiology, so no mechanism is established; laboratory communication task may not generalise to real conversation.

studies.title: Eye-movement therapy works even when you are not consciously thinking about the memory
studies.ns_score_reason: directly challenges a core assumption of EMDR, with objective physiological outcomes; limited by being a lab fear-conditioning analogue, not clinical trauma.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Participants were fear-conditioned to snake/spider images, then re-exposed to those cues either passively (Experiment 1, N=56) or subliminally (Experiment 2, N=83) while performing smooth-pursuit eye movements. Passive re-exposure cut skin conductance responses during the session and 24 hours later; subliminal re-exposure did not change immediate physiology but reduced the frequency and emotional intensity of intrusive thoughts over the following week — and people reported markedly less distress during the unconscious version.
studies.why_it_matters: EMDR protocols assume the patient must actively hold the traumatic memory in mind; if reactivation below awareness is sufficient, treatment could in principle be made far less aversive — a hypothesis that now needs testing in actual patients.
studies.pitch_angle: "Could trauma therapy work without you having to relive the trauma?" Open on the dropout problem: many people quit exposure-based therapy because it hurts. Lead with the finding that the *less* distressing subliminal condition still cut intrusive thoughts for a week. Call Yang Wang's group at Zhejiang University, and get a sceptical EMDR researcher to say why lab-conditioned spider fear is not PTSD.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychology or long-read outlet: EMDR's decades-long mechanism controversy — is the eye movement doing anything, is it just working memory taxation, and why has a therapy this widely used remained this poorly explained?
studies.caveats: Analogue fear conditioning in non-clinical volunteers, not trauma patients; short follow-up (24 hours / 1 week); intrusive-thought outcomes are self-reported; no clinical claim can be made.

studies.title: Wait 27 seconds and your short-term memory starts inventing words that were never there
studies.ns_score_reason: clean, vivid demonstration that false memories form within seconds, and it survives explicit warnings; incremental to a much-studied paradigm.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a short-term-memory version of the classic Deese/Roediger–McDermott false-memory task: five-word lists followed by recognition tests either immediately or after 3, 9 or 27 seconds of distraction. True recognition fell as the delay grew while false recognition *rose* — and the illusion appeared even with no delay at all, and even when participants were explicitly warned that semantically related lures were coming and told not to be fooled.
studies.why_it_matters: False memory is usually framed as something that creeps in over days; this places its onset within the first half-minute and shows warning people does not protect them.
studies.pitch_angle: "Your memory starts distorting the moment you stop paying attention." Open on a witness statement taken 30 seconds after an incident. The hook: forewarning doesn't help. Call Guillermo Campoy at the University of Murcia and ask what phonological versus semantic traces decaying at different rates means for eyewitness protocols.
studies.wider_angle: For a law-and-science outlet: the "immediate recall is reliable" assumption embedded in police first-account procedures, and whether the seconds-scale distortion curve should change how first accounts are taken and weighted.
studies.caveats: Not preregistered; word-list laboratory paradigm with limited ecological reach; student-heavy sample likely.

studies.title: To remember to do something later, physically rehearse it — imagining it doesn't help
studies.ns_score_reason: large lifespan sample and a genuinely negative result for a strategy the field has been promoting; single lab task limits reach.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: 373 participants — children (n=90), adolescents (n=96), young adults (n=97) and middle-aged adults (n=90) — were randomly assigned to form intentions using episodic future thinking (mentally simulating the future action), enactment encoding (physically performing it), or standard encoding, then completed a computerised prospective-memory task. Enactment beat both other conditions across every age group; episodic future thinking gave no benefit over standard encoding at all.
studies.why_it_matters: Episodic future thinking is a popular recommendation for improving intention memory; this well-powered comparison finds the physical rehearsal wins and the mental simulation does nothing, at least under high ongoing task demand.
studies.pitch_angle: "Don't visualise it — do it." Open on the universal failure of remembering to take the medication / post the letter / send the email. The surprise is that the widely touted mental-simulation trick failed while a crude physical run-through worked, from age 8 to 60. Call Mareike Altgassen at Mainz and ask whether cue focality explains the null.
studies.wider_angle: A practical, service-y piece for a general health outlet on the science of prospective memory in medication adherence — an area where forgetting has measurable clinical costs — including what enactment might look like in a real routine.
studies.caveats: Single computerised task; randomised but not, as reported, preregistered; the null for episodic future thinking may be task-specific (the authors themselves invoke cue focality and ongoing task load).

studies.title: Taking notes you expect to keep makes you encode less deeply than a deliberately shallow task
studies.journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
studies.ns_score_reason: four experiments with a striking benchmark comparison; laboratory word lists rather than real study material.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Across four experiments, participants either offloaded information into notes (expecting or not expecting to lose access at test) or encoded under deep- versus shallow-processing instructions. When access to notes was unexpectedly removed, recall was *worse* than in the shallow-processing condition. A fourth experiment showed people made fewer "remember" (vivid recollection) judgements when their notes were available at test — access changed the subjective quality of retrieval, not just its accuracy.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a number on the cost of externalising memory: expecting a backup can leave you encoding below the level of someone doing a deliberately superficial task, and it thins out the felt richness of what you do recall.
studies.pitch_angle: "Your phone isn't just holding your memories — it's stopping them forming." Open on the panic of losing a notes app before an exam or meeting. Lead with the benchmark: worse than shallow processing. Call Lauren Richmond at Stony Brook, and pair this with the offloading-under-overload paper (PMID 42607389) for a balanced piece on when offloading helps and when it hollows you out.
studies.wider_angle: An education-sector feature on laptop notetaking, lecture recording and AI meeting summaries: institutions are systematically engineering the "expected access" condition that this work shows suppresses encoding. Fits an education or technology outlet.
studies.caveats: Laboratory word-list recall; effects on real-world learning untested; sample sizes and demographics not reported in the abstract.

studies.title: Eye-movement therapy dampens shame, anger and sadness memories, not just fear
studies.ns_score_reason: big sample and a clean null on the moderator that most theories predicted; online, single-session, self-report only.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: 560 participants were randomly assigned to recall an autobiographical memory dominated by fear, shame, anger or sadness, and then either performed eye movements while recalling (dual task) or simply recalled it. Dual-task recall produced the largest drops in memory vividness and unpleasantness across all four emotions, and the dominant emotion did not reliably moderate the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: PTSD is increasingly recognised as not purely fear-based; this suggests the dual-task mechanism is emotion-general, which matters for treating moral injury and shame-dominated trauma.
studies.pitch_angle: "Trauma isn't just fear — and the standard therapy trick seems to know that." Open on a patient whose defining trauma emotion is humiliation, not terror. Call Kevin van Schie at Tilburg and ask what a well-powered null moderator result tells us about the working-memory-taxation account.
studies.wider_angle: For a mental-health or feature outlet: the quiet reclassification of PTSD away from a fear disorder, and what that means for moral injury in veterans, healthcare workers and abuse survivors.
studies.caveats: Online proof-of-principle, single session; outcomes entirely self-rated (vividness, unpleasantness, accessibility); non-clinical autobiographical memories; no follow-up.

studies.title: A third of online study participants wander off mid-task — and it shows in their memory scores
studies.ns_score_reason: two pre-registered experiments with an internal replication, and it lands squarely on the credibility of a huge slice of published psychology.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Two pre-registered experiments tracked whether Amazon Mechanical Turk participants navigated away from the study page during the encoding phase of a memory task. Roughly one third went off task, and doing so predicted worse memory performance. Experiment 2 replicated this and found that an explicit warning reduced page-switching but did not reduce the *proportion of time* spent off task.
studies.why_it_matters: Since the pandemic, a large fraction of published cognitive and mental-health research has been collected online; this quantifies a systematic, performance-degrading contaminant in that data — and shows the obvious fix doesn't work.
studies.pitch_angle: "A third of the people in your favourite online psychology study weren't looking at the screen." Open on the mundane image of a paid participant checking their email during a memory test. Lead with the failed warning manipulation. Call Daniel Peterson at Skidmore; ask how much of the recent literature he thinks is affected and what a workable attention check would look like.
studies.wider_angle: A meta-science piece for a research-culture or science-policy outlet on the post-2020 migration of behavioural science to crowdsourcing platforms, gig-economy incentives for speed over care, and whether journals should require off-task telemetry.
studies.caveats: MTurk-specific — may not generalise to Prolific or other panels; page-switching is a proxy for attention and misses phone use; effect sizes on memory not given in the abstract.

studies.title: Notetaking rescues an overloaded working memory — but people botch their own notes
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful replication-plus-extension with a nice twist on offloading errors, but the core benefit is unsurprising.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Participants performed a letter-string task at loads of four, eight and 12 items, with or without the option to type notes. Offloading improved performance and the benefit grew with load, peaking at 12 items. But people also made more offloading-specific errors at high load — copying items down wrong, or misreading their own notes at recall.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes offloading as a strategy with its own error mode rather than a clean workaround, which is relevant to anyone designing checklists or handover procedures under pressure.
studies.pitch_angle: "Writing it down saves you — until you write it down wrong." Open on a nurse or air-traffic controller scribbling a handover under load. Call Alexandra Morrison at Sacramento State and pair her with the Stony Brook offloading group for a two-sided piece on the arithmetic of when to trust your notes.
studies.wider_angle: A human-factors feature for a safety, aviation or healthcare-quality publication: the error taxonomy of transcription under cognitive load, and why checklist design increasingly assumes offloading is free.
studies.caveats: Sample size not reported in the abstract; abstract laboratory letter-string task; individual-difference analyses were all null.

studies.title: A week of brain stimulation improves both sleep and overnight skill consolidation in insomnia
studies.ns_score_reason: randomised and double-blind with a memory outcome rather than just sleep scores, but very small and single-site.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Forty-two people with insomnia were randomised, double-blind, to seven consecutive days of active or sham transcranial direct current stimulation. The active group showed significantly better sleep quality (PSQI) and significantly greater offline consolidation of implicit sequence learning than sham, with no improvement in the sham group.
studies.why_it_matters: Most insomnia interventions are judged on sleep scores alone; showing a parallel gain in memory consolidation would give a functional reason to care, if it replicates at scale.
studies.pitch_angle: "Treating insomnia may restore the memory work sleep is supposed to do." Open on someone with chronic insomnia who describes their real complaint as not tiredness but that nothing sticks. Call the Northwest Normal University group and ask an independent tDCS methodologist about blinding integrity in a seven-session protocol.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or technology outlet: the consumer neurostimulation market is already selling sleep devices; a piece on the gap between small academic tDCS trials and what is on sale, and what regulators require.
studies.caveats: N=42, well under 100; single centre; sleep quality is self-reported (PSQI) with no polysomnography; no follow-up beyond post-intervention; tDCS blinding is notoriously imperfect.

studies.title: Acting out an instruction helps you remember it — even if you have never seen anything
studies.ns_score_reason: a rarely tested population gives a clean theoretical answer; small N and an odd sub-result in the residual-vision group.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Fifty-one participants — with total vision loss, residual vision, or typical vision — recalled spoken instructions either after hearing them only or after physically enacting them. Enactment improved recall in all three groups with no significant difference by visual acuity, though people with residual vision appeared to benefit least.
studies.why_it_matters: The enactment effect has been widely attributed to visual imagery of the action; this suggests kinaesthetic encoding alone can carry it, which matters for how instructions are designed for blind users.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why doing beats hearing — even in the dark." Open on the practical question of how a blind person memorises a multi-step procedure. Lead with the theoretical kill: the enactment effect does not need vision. Call Elvira Masoura at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, and ask about the puzzling residual-vision result.
studies.wider_angle: An accessibility-design story for a technology or disability-focused outlet: voice assistants and screen readers deliver instructions as pure speech, and this suggests they are using the weakest available channel.
studies.caveats: N=51, small and unevenly divided across three groups; the residual-vision finding is exploratory; single-site; participants with visual impairment are a heterogeneous group.

studies.title: You remember cheaters' faces — not just the photos you saw them in
studies.ns_score_reason: closes a real methodological loophole in the cheater-detection literature; a confirmation rather than a reversal.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Previous studies showing that people have better source memory for individuals who behaved dishonestly used the *same* photograph at learning and test, raising the possibility participants were remembering picture details rather than people. This experiment changed the viewing perspective of the faces between learning and test, and still found a source-memory advantage for cheaters in both the changed-perspective and identical-photo conditions.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts the cheater-memory effect from a possible artefact of image matching to genuine person recognition, shoring up an evolutionary-psychology claim that has been methodologically vulnerable.
studies.pitch_angle: "Your brain really does keep a list of who ripped you off." Open on the experience of recognising someone months later and immediately recalling that they let you down. Call Mirjam Kroneisen at RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau and press on how large the effect is and whether it survives long delays.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest or social-science outlet on reputation as cognitive infrastructure — from village gossip to online seller ratings — and whether digital reputation systems are outsourcing a memory system we evolved to run internally.
studies.caveats: Sample size not reported in the abstract; single laboratory experiment; artificial reputational vignettes; short retention interval.

studies.title: Handwriting a new word by hand shapes how strongly it lodges in the mental lexicon overnight
studies.ns_score_reason: technically impressive EEG-plus-pen-kinematics co-registration with an overnight behavioural payoff; the story is subtle to tell.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Sixty-three native Spanish speakers learned novel words by writing them repeatedly while EEG and pen kinematics were recorded simultaneously. Spelling knowledge plateaued after roughly four exposures, but motor refinement of the handwriting continued improving across all encounters — the two processes did not track each other. Crucially, the size of the exposure-driven neural change during learning predicted how strongly the new word competed with real words in a lexical decision test after a night's sleep.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete neural handle on the long-argued claim that handwriting supports word learning, and separates the orthographic from the motor part of the process.
studies.pitch_angle: "Four goes to learn the spelling; much longer for the hand to catch up." Open on a child learning to write a new word, or an adult learning a foreign script. Lead with the dissociation and the overnight prediction. Call Yang Fu at Shanghai International Studies University.
studies.wider_angle: For an education outlet: the handwriting-versus-keyboard debate in schools has been fought largely on weak correlational evidence; this is the kind of mechanistic data that could settle parts of it, and it deserves a sober audit of what is and isn't known.
studies.caveats: N=63; single language and script; novel pseudowords rather than real vocabulary; the sleep link is correlational (neural modulation predicted, but sleep was not manipulated).

studies.title: Cognitive training in schizophrenia shifts brain waves, memory and sweat responses together
studies.ns_score_reason: prospectively registered RCT combining EEG, autonomic and behavioural outcomes, but modest N and an unspecified control condition.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Fifty-seven clinically stable outpatients with schizophrenia were randomised to 12 weeks of Cognitive Remediation Therapy (24 sessions) or control; 48 completed. The CRT group showed larger P300 amplitudes, increased frontal midline theta during a 2-back task, reduced skin-conductance reactivity to negative images, and better working memory, emotion recognition, symptom scores and quality of life. Neural gains correlated with cognitive gains; autonomic changes correlated with emotion-regulation gains.
studies.why_it_matters: Cognitive remediation is known to help behaviourally; showing convergent neural and autonomic change makes it harder to dismiss as practice effects and points to which mechanisms to target.
studies.pitch_angle: "Brain training that actually changes the brain — in schizophrenia." Open on the fact that antipsychotics do almost nothing for the cognitive symptoms that most predict whether someone can work. Call Metin Çınaroğlu at Istanbul Nişantaşı University and ask what the control group actually did.
studies.wider_angle: A health-services piece for a specialist psychiatry or health outlet: cognitive remediation has decent evidence but is barely available in most systems — why psychosocial interventions with mechanistic support still lose out to prescribing.
studies.caveats: N=57 randomised, 48 completed — under 100; single centre; control condition not characterised in the abstract (possibly no active comparator, so expectancy effects are plausible); many secondary outcomes without stated correction.

studies.title: Daily diaries show mood and PTSD symptoms move together within a day — but not into the next
studies.ns_score_reason: the null cross-day result is genuinely useful against a common clinical assumption, but the design is uncontrolled and the sample small.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Seventy trauma-exposed adults completed 21 daily surveys before and after four sessions of the Processing of Positive Memories Technique — a therapy built around retrieving detailed positive autobiographical memories. Negative affect, low positive affect and trauma-related cognitions tracked same-day symptom severity strongly, but none predicted next-day symptoms once prior-day symptoms were accounted for. The same-day negative-affect–symptom coupling weakened after the intervention.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that "a bad day today means a worse day tomorrow" is not how PTSD symptoms actually propagate at the daily timescale — and that a therapy may work by loosening within-day coupling rather than by lowering average distress.
studies.pitch_angle: "A therapy for trauma built entirely on good memories." Open on the counterintuitive clinical instruction: don't talk about the trauma, talk in the present tense about a good day. Lead with the finding that today's bad mood doesn't forecast tomorrow. Call Ateka Contractor at the University of North Texas.
studies.wider_angle: For a methods-literate outlet: ecological momentary assessment is quietly overturning cross-sectional assumptions about how symptoms cause each other, and clinical theory has not caught up.
studies.caveats: N=70; all outcomes self-reported; the daily-diary analysis has no control arm (the RCT comparison is reported elsewhere); interrupted-time-series result is marginal (p=.035); trauma-exposed volunteers may not represent treatment-seeking populations.

studies.title: A fourth "perception–memory pair" turns up in the parietal lobe
studies.ns_score_reason: a tidy extension of an elegant organisational principle, replicated across two datasets, but tiny N and a hard sell to non-specialists.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Across two independent fMRI datasets (total N=24, 14 female) using different stimuli and memory tasks, recalling visual scenes reliably activated a region just in front of a recently discovered scene-perception area in superior parietal cortex. At rest, the perception area coupled with other perception areas and the memory area with other memory areas, and the perception area sat at the junction of four streams linking egocentric vision, map-based navigation, perspective taking and goal-directed movement.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the brain systematically builds paired perception-and-memory regions across the cortical surface — a repeating architectural motif for stitching what you see onto what you remember about a place.
studies.pitch_angle: "The brain keeps building the same circuit over and over." Open on walking into a familiar room and instantly knowing what's around the corner. The hook is the repeating motif rather than the region itself. Call Adam Steel at Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
studies.wider_angle: A navigation feature for a science or technology outlet: how the brain's place-memory machinery maps onto — and diverges from — the way robots and self-driving systems fuse live sensing with stored maps.
studies.caveats: N=24 total across two datasets; fMRI localisation only, no causal manipulation; region naming and boundaries in this part of parietal cortex remain contested.

studies.title: Harder-looking Chinese characters are easier to pull out of short-term memory
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely odd results with a language-specific hook; three experiments but a narrow paradigm and no sample details.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Using the Sternberg short-term memory scanning paradigm across three experiments, researchers varied stroke count, phonetic regularity and semantic transparency of Chinese characters. Simpler characters were retrieved more accurately, as expected — but characters whose pronunciation is *not* predictable from their phonetic component, and characters whose meaning is *not* transparent from their parts, were retrieved more accurately than their "helpful" counterparts.
studies.why_it_matters: It hints that predictability in a writing system can create interference rather than support during memory retrieval — a result that pushes against the assumption that regularity always aids processing.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why the more confusing Chinese characters are easier to hold in mind." Open on the intuition that a logographic script must be harder to remember, and then invert it. Call Hongli Li at Anyang Normal University, and get a psycholinguist working on alphabetic scripts to say whether the same logic should apply to irregular English spellings.
studies.wider_angle: For a language or education outlet: what writing-system differences reveal about the supposed universals of reading and memory, and why so much of cognitive psychology's evidence base rests on English.
studies.caveats: Sample size, age range and preregistration status not reported in the abstract; Sternberg paradigm is far from natural reading; results need replication in alphabetic scripts before general claims.

studies.title: Targeted brain stimulation moves a network — but not the memory it was aimed at
studies.ns_score_reason: the dissociation between network change and behavioural non-change is the interesting bit, but it is a single case.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: In a randomised placebo-controlled single-case protocol, a patient with posterior cortical atrophy — an atypical, visually dominated form of Alzheimer's — received intermittent theta-burst stimulation to a personally identified left caudal middle frontal target chosen for its connectivity to the default mode network. Active stimulation increased connectivity between the target and distributed DMN regions as predicted, but associative memory did not improve; visuospatial working memory did.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a clean, honestly reported example of the gap between shifting a brain network and shifting behaviour, which is the central unresolved problem in therapeutic brain stimulation.
studies.pitch_angle: "We moved the network. The memory didn't budge." Open on the seductive logic of personalised, connectivity-guided TMS, then the result. Call Mark Eldaief or Alexandra Touroutoglou at MGH and ask what the unexpected visuospatial gain implies about targeting.
studies.wider_angle: For a neurology or medical outlet: posterior cortical atrophy itself — a form of Alzheimer's that presents as a problem with seeing rather than remembering, and is routinely misdiagnosed by opticians and ophthalmologists.
studies.caveats: N=1; no generalisability; secondary outcome improvement in a single case is at high risk of chance; short follow-up.

studies.title: A nine-week course improves how older adults read between the lines — and the gains stick
studies.ns_score_reason: targets a neglected and highly relatable ability with three-month persistence, but no control group at all.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Twenty-four healthy adults aged 65–86 completed a nine-week group programme (Advanced Cognitive Pragmatic Treatment) aimed at pragmatic communication — irony, hints, gesture, tone, context-appropriate speech. Pragmatic comprehension and production improved from pre- to post-training and were maintained at three months, in both linguistic and extralinguistic channels. Attention, memory, processing speed, executive function and theory of mind were unchanged, suggesting the gains were specific rather than a general cognitive lift.
studies.why_it_matters: Age-related decline in reading social subtext gets far less attention than memory decline despite mattering enormously for isolation and independence — and the specificity of the effect argues against it being generic practice benefit.
studies.pitch_angle: "The bit of ageing nobody trains: getting the joke." Open on an older adult who takes a sarcastic remark literally and feels the room shift. The hook is that the unchanged memory and theory-of-mind scores are the *good* news here. Call Francesca Bosco or Ilaria Gabbatore at Turin.
studies.wider_angle: For an ageing or social-policy outlet: loneliness interventions overwhelmingly focus on opportunity (clubs, befriending) rather than capability; a piece on training the communicative skills that make contact rewarding.
studies.caveats: N=24; no control group, so practice, expectancy and group-attendance effects cannot be separated; explicitly described by the authors as preliminary; healthy, self-selected volunteers.

studies.title: Training working memory with emotional material curbs risky decisions in heavy internet users
studies.ns_score_reason: randomised with a one-month follow-up and an active comparator, but the sample is very small for the claims made.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Thirty university students with problematic internet use were randomised to 20 sessions of emotional working memory training (n=15) or feature-matching control training (n=15). At post-test and one-month follow-up, the trained group showed reduced problematic internet use symptoms, less risky decision-making and fewer maladaptive emotion-regulation strategies; adaptive strategies did not change.
studies.why_it_matters: Working memory training has a poor record of transferring to anything useful; a result showing transfer to emotion regulation and decision-making is notable — but at this sample size it is a hypothesis, not a finding.
studies.pitch_angle: "Brain training's best shot yet — with an emotional twist." Open on the graveyard of failed working memory training studies and ask why adding emotional content might change the calculus. Call Sanaz Eyni at the University of Kurdistan and pair with a transfer sceptic such as Monica Melby-Lervåg or Zach Hambrick for balance.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology or student-focused outlet: the shift in problematic-internet-use research from abstinence framing to targeting the underlying emotion-regulation deficit — and whether "digital detox" is the wrong intervention entirely.
studies.caveats: N=30 total, 15 per arm — badly underpowered; outcomes largely self-reported; single site; university students only; one-month follow-up is short.

studies.title: Personalised symptom networks reveal four recurring "shapes" of PTSD
studies.ns_score_reason: an interesting bridge between individual and group-level psychopathology with intensive data, but the story is abstract and methods-heavy.
studies.media_check: Not verified — no SerpAPI key configured
studies.the_study: Fifty-five trauma-exposed people (31 with PTSD) chose personalised items representing the components of Ehlers and Clark's cognitive model — trauma memory, triggers, negative appraisals, sense of current threat, coping strategies. Forty-one completed three weeks of ecological momentary assessment (2,594 observations). Individual networks confirmed the model's central claim that "sense of current threat" is the hub, and clustering the individual networks revealed four recurring formulation subtypes: threat-reactive, appraisal-centred, memory-centred, and trigger–threat-driven.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a route out of the long-standing problem that group averages describe nobody, by showing that person-specific networks still fall into a small number of recognisable patterns — which, if it holds, could inform which component a therapist targets first.
studies.pitch_angle: "There isn't one PTSD — there are four shapes of it." Open on two patients with identical diagnoses whose symptoms are driven by entirely different engines. Call Tim Dalgleish at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit in Cambridge and ask whether subtype-matched treatment is testable now.
studies.wider_angle: For a science-of-medicine outlet: the personalised-psychiatry debate — intensive smartphone data promises individually tailored models, but almost none have yet been shown to improve outcomes. A sober audit of that gap.
studies.caveats: N=55 recruited, only 41 completed EMA — small for cluster analysis; clusters are exploratory and unreplicated; all data self-reported via momentary assessment; no treatment outcomes measured; substantial simulation/methods component.

citation_table.journal: J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch converge on the same trade-off: memory is built by physical action, and weakened when action is outsourced. "To remember to do something later, physically rehearse it — imagining it doesn't help" (PMID 42627881) found enactment beat mental simulation at every age from 8 to 60; "Acting out an instruction helps you remember it — even if you have never seen anything" (PMID 42622513) showed the enactment effect survives total blindness, so it is kinaesthetic rather than visual; and "Handwriting a new word by hand shapes how strongly it lodges in the mental lexicon overnight" (PMID 42607453) gives the motor route a neural signature that predicts overnight lexical integration. Against that, "Taking notes you expect to keep makes you encode less deeply than a deliberately shallow task" (PMID 42622798) shows expected external access suppresses encoding below the level of deliberately superficial processing, while "Notetaking rescues an overloaded working memory — but people botch their own notes" (PMID 42607389) shows offloading genuinely rescues an overloaded system but generates its own transcription and misreading errors.

**Why pitch this now:** Institutions are currently engineering the exact "expected access" condition these studies flag as corrosive — lecture recording, AI meeting summaries, voice assistants, screen readers delivering instructions as pure speech — while simultaneously stripping out the handwriting and physical rehearsal that the other half of the evidence says does the encoding work.

**Angle:** A feature on the emerging cognitive arithmetic of when to use your body and when to use your device: memory as something enacted rather than stored, with a hard-nosed audit of where offloading genuinely buys capacity (high load, checklists, handovers) and where it quietly hollows out learning. Aimed at general readers who take notes for a living, plus an education and workplace-technology readership.

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — fits the Mind slot's appetite for a counterintuitive, mechanism-led take on everyday behaviour, and lets the blind-participant enactment result carry the theoretical punch rather than a lifestyle framing.
- **BBC Future** — built for exactly this "what the science says about how you should actually take notes" register, with a global education and productivity audience.
- **The Atlantic (Technology or Family/Education)** — has repeatedly run the handwriting-versus-keyboard and phones-and-memory arguments; this batch supplies the mechanistic evidence those essays have been missing, including the AI-summary angle.
- **Wired** — the "AI is now the default note-taker" hook, framed as an unexamined design decision with measurable cognitive costs, including the accessibility point about voice interfaces using the weakest encoding channel.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Memory — August 2026
**Checked:** 2026-08-22 | **Studies reviewed:** 21
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-08-22

---

### Study 1: Semaglutide is linked to fewer cognitive complaints in people with psychiatric illness
**PMID:** 42624612 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Cohort description implies everyone started a drug** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "researchers compared 13,007 adults with a psychiatric diagnosis who started an antidiabetic drug"
- **Abstract says:** "Semaglutide initiation was compared against four comparator strategies including sitagliptin, empagliflozin, glipizide or no antidiabetic treatment."
- **Problem:** One of the four comparator strategies is *no* antidiabetic treatment, so the cohort cannot be described as uniformly drug initiators.
- **Suggested fix:** "researchers compared 13,007 adults with a psychiatric diagnosis across four treatment strategies — semaglutide (n=1261), sitagliptin, empagliflozin, glipizide or no antidiabetic treatment"

**Issue B. Omits the null comparison with sitagliptin** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "clinician-rated cognitive signs/symptoms … were lower with semaglutide than with no antidiabetic treatment (mean ratio 0.75), glipizide or empagliflozin"
- **Abstract says:** "lower but not significantly different from sitagliptin (12.52; MR, 0.89 (0.77–1.02); p=0.50)"
- **Problem:** Three of four comparisons were significant and one — against the other incretin-adjacent agent — was not. Omitting it makes the signal look more uniform than it is, and the sitagliptin null is the comparison most relevant to whether this is GLP-1-specific.
- **Suggested fix:** Add: "…but not significantly different from sitagliptin (MR 0.89, p=0.50)."

**Issue C. Major-depression finding recast as a stronger effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "with the strongest signal in memory and in people with major depression"
- **Abstract says:** "Similar effect sizes were seen across disorders but were only consistently significant in major depression."
- **Problem:** Effect sizes were comparable across diagnoses; major depression stood out only in statistical significance (plausibly a power artefact of the larger subgroup). "Strongest signal in people with major depression" implies a differential biological effect the study did not find.
- **Suggested fix:** "with the strongest signal in memory; effect sizes were similar across diagnoses but reached significance consistently only in major depression, likely reflecting subgroup size."

*NS fit 7/10 is defensible — very large cohort, clinician-rated (not self-reported) outcome, observational status clearly flagged. Industry conflicts are correctly carried into Caveats.*

---

### Study 2: Sleep sharpens memory for who told you what
**PMID:** 42492165 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Word-reduction effect attributed to both experiments** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Sleepers showed better item recognition *and* better source memory … and used fewer words to describe previously discussed items"
- **Abstract says:** "The Sleep group also used fewer words to describe old vs. new items in Experiment 2"
- **Problem:** The recognition/source-memory effect held across Experiments 1 and 2; the communicative-efficiency effect is reported only for the face-to-face Experiment 2. As written it reads as a general finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "…and, in the face-to-face experiment only, used fewer words to describe previously discussed items."

*NS fit 7/10 is defensible: three experiments, an experimental sleep/wake manipulation, and the null mechanism result is honestly flagged in both the score rationale and Caveats.*

---

### Study 3: Eye-movement therapy works even when you are not consciously thinking about the memory
**PMID:** 42531952 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts a clinical claim the Caveats disown** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** Headline: "Eye-movement therapy works even when you are not consciously thinking about the memory"
- **Abstract says:** Participants "acquired conditioned fear to snake/spider images"; findings "suggest a promising noninvasive strategy" — i.e. an analogue paradigm in non-clinical volunteers.
- **Problem:** The Caveats correctly state "no clinical claim can be made", but the headline states flatly that a therapy "works". Nothing in this study tested therapy in patients; it tested a fear-conditioning analogue.
- **Suggested fix:** "Eye movements dampened lab-induced fear even when the cue was shown below awareness"

**Issue B. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "NS fit: 7/10"
- **Problem:** The headline-grabbing arm (subliminal re-exposure) rests on self-reported intrusive thoughts over a week, with a *null* on the objective physiological measure. That is thinner evidence than a 7 implies for a claim about trauma therapy.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the rationale noting the objective outcome was null in the subliminal condition.

---

### Study 4: Wait 27 seconds and your short-term memory starts inventing words
**PMID:** 42277491 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline and "Why it matters" locate onset later than the data do** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "Wait 27 seconds and your short-term memory starts inventing words that were never there"; "this places its onset within the first half-minute"
- **Abstract says:** "it can be observed even with no delay and no intervening distraction between study and test"
- **Problem:** The digest's own body text says the illusion appeared with no delay at all, which contradicts the headline's implication that 27 seconds is the trigger point. The delay effect is about *growth* in false recognition, not onset.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Your memory invents words within seconds — and warning people doesn't stop it." Why it matters: "false recognition is present immediately and grows over the first half-minute."

*Sample size and true/false direction are correctly reported; non-preregistration is confirmed in the abstract's declarations.*

---

### Study 5: To remember to do something later, physically rehearse it
**PMID:** 42627881 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Null age interaction reported as a per-group effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Enactment beat both other conditions across every age group"
- **Abstract says:** "participants in the EE condition outperformed those in both the EFT and standard encoding conditions, with no evidence that this benefit differed by age group"
- **Problem:** A significant main effect plus a non-significant interaction is not the same as a demonstrated benefit within each of the four age groups.
- **Suggested fix:** "Enactment beat both other conditions overall, with no evidence the benefit differed by age."

**Issue B. Age range in pitch not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a crude physical run-through worked, from age 8 to 60"
- **Abstract says:** Group labels only — children, adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults; no ages given.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only, and stated as fact.
- **Suggested fix:** "…worked from childhood to middle age (confirm exact age bands from full text)."

---

### Study 6: Taking notes you expect to keep makes you encode less deeply
**PMID:** 42622798 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Pitch overstates the encoding effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Your phone isn't just holding your memories — it's stopping them forming."
- **Abstract says:** "performance in the unexpected loss of access offloading conditions was poorer than performance in the shallow encoding conditions"
- **Problem:** Recall was reduced relative to a shallow-processing benchmark, not abolished. "Stopping them forming" is hype beyond a graded recall difference in a word-list task.
- **Suggested fix:** "Your phone isn't just holding your memories — it's thinning out how well they form."

*Experiment structure (3 encoding experiments + 1 remember/know experiment) and the remember-judgement result are reported accurately.*

---

### Study 7: Eye-movement therapy dampens shame, anger and sadness memories
**PMID:** 42622123 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Therapy" in the headline for an online analogue task** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "Eye-movement therapy dampens shame, anger and sadness memories, not just fear"
- **Abstract says:** "the present online proof-of-principle study"; outcomes were self-rated vividness, unpleasantness and accessibility of everyday autobiographical memories.
- **Problem:** Caveats flag this, but the headline still frames a single-session online dual-task manipulation as therapy delivered to trauma memories.
- **Suggested fix:** "The eye-movement trick in EMDR dulls shame, anger and sadness memories too — at least in the lab"

**Issue B. Novelty label and strength of conclusion** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: Overturns prior research"; "this suggests the dual-task mechanism is emotion-general"
- **Abstract says:** "These findings tentatively suggest that dual-task interventions can be applied to emotionally diverse autobiographical memories."
- **Problem:** A non-significant moderator is absence of evidence, not evidence of emotion-generality, and the authors hedge with "tentatively". "Overturns prior research" overstates a null moderation result.
- **Suggested fix:** Novelty: "Challenges a prediction"; Why it matters: "this tentatively suggests the dual-task effect is not specific to fear."

---

### Study 8: A third of online study participants wander off mid-task
**PMID:** 42608507 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Pre-registration, the one-third estimate, the direction of the performance effect, and the Experiment 2 warning result (reduced page switching but not proportion of time off task) all match the abstract. MTurk-specificity and the absence of reported effect sizes are correctly flagged in Caveats.

---

### Study 9: Notetaking rescues an overloaded working memory
**PMID:** 42607389 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Error rate framed as load-dependent** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "But people also made more offloading-specific errors at high load"
- **Abstract says:** "Participants offloaded more frequently at higher loads. However, they also made more offloading-related errors by incorrectly copying information or incorrectly reading and/or reporting notes when tested."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not explicitly state that offloading errors *increased with set size* — only that they occurred. The load-dependence is inferred. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "But people also made offloading-specific errors — copying items down wrong, or misreading their own notes at recall (check full text for whether these scaled with load)."

---

### Study 10: A week of brain stimulation improves both sleep and overnight skill consolidation
**PMID:** 42537590 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Overnight" consolidation not specified in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "…improves both sleep and overnight skill consolidation in insomnia"
- **Abstract says:** "offline consolidation of implicit sequence learning", assessed before and after the 7-day intervention.
- **Problem:** "Offline consolidation" is not stated to be an overnight (sleep-bracketed) interval in the abstract; the digest converts a generic term into a sleep-dependent one, which is also the more headline-friendly reading. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "…improves sleep and offline consolidation of a motor sequence skill in insomnia" (confirm the consolidation interval from full text before pitching the sleep link).

*N=42, randomisation, double-blinding and the sham null are all accurately reported, and the small N is properly flagged in Caveats and the NS score.*

---

### Study 11: Acting out an instruction helps you remember it
**PMID:** 42622513 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Group-wise effect inferred from a null group difference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Enactment improved recall in all three groups with no significant difference by visual acuity"
- **Abstract says:** "enactment produced higher recall accuracy than spoken input alone, but no significant differences were found across visual acuity groups"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports an overall enactment advantage and no group differences; it does not report a significant within-group enactment effect for each of the three groups separately (n≈17 per group).
- **Suggested fix:** "Enactment improved recall overall, with no significant differences between the three visual-acuity groups."

*N=51, the three-group structure, and the residual-vision oddity are reported accurately, and the small, uneven groups are flagged.*

---

### Study 12: You remember cheaters' faces
**PMID:** 42625545 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Used the same photograph" stated absolutely** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Previous studies showing that people have better source memory for individuals who behaved dishonestly used the *same* photograph at learning and test"
- **Abstract says:** "in most of these experiments, the same facial images were used during both the learning and testing phases"
- **Problem:** "Most" becomes "used" — a small hardening of the methodological critique.
- **Suggested fix:** "…most of which used the same photograph at learning and test."

*The main result — source-memory advantage for cheaters in both the changed-perspective and identical-photo conditions — is reported accurately, and the missing N is flagged.*

---

### Study 13: Handwriting a new word shapes how strongly it lodges in the mental lexicon
**PMID:** 42607453 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal verb in headline for a predictive relationship** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "Handwriting a new word by hand shapes how strongly it lodges in the mental lexicon overnight"
- **Abstract says:** "the magnitude of exposure-induced neural modulation during learning predicted the strength of subsequent lexical competition … after overnight consolidation"
- **Problem:** The relationship is predictive/correlational (neural modulation → later lexical competition); handwriting itself was not manipulated against a non-handwriting condition. Caveats note the sleep link is correlational, but the headline still reads causally.
- **Suggested fix:** "How much the brain changes while you handwrite a new word predicts how well it lodges in the lexicon overnight"

*N=63, native Spanish speakers, the four-exposure orthographic asymptote and the protracted motor trajectory are all accurate.*

---

### Study 14: Cognitive training in schizophrenia shifts brain waves, memory and sweat responses
**PMID:** 42625165 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Randomisation (57 → 48 completers), the 12-week/24-session protocol, P300 as primary outcome, theta, SCR, working memory, emotion recognition, PANSS and QLS gains, and the two correlation patterns all match. Prospective registration, the modest N and the uncharacterised control condition are correctly flagged.

---

### Study 15: Daily diaries show mood and PTSD symptoms move together within a day
**PMID:** 42623486 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Publication date presented without the issue date** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Published: 20 Aug 2026"; citation table "2026-08-20"
- **Abstract says:** "Eur J Psychotraumatol. 2026 Dec;17(1):2703327 … Epub 2026 Aug 20."
- **Problem:** 20 Aug is the epub date; the issue date is Dec 2026. Other entries in the digest (2, 3, 4, 10) use the "issue (epub)" convention, so this one is inconsistent.
- **Suggested fix:** "Published: Dec 2026 (online 20 Aug 2026)"

*N=70, the 21 daily surveys, four PPMT sessions, the same-day ps<.001, the next-day null after adjusting for prior-day symptoms, and the p=.035 interrupted-time-series result are all accurate, and the absence of a control arm is flagged.*

---

### Study 16: A fourth "perception–memory pair" turns up in the parietal lobe
**PMID:** 42624782 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Anatomical description incomplete** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a region just in front of a recently discovered scene-perception area in superior parietal cortex"
- **Abstract says:** "a region (referred to here as SPMA) immediately anterior *and dorsal* to SPA"
- **Problem:** Drops the dorsal component of the localisation. Trivial for a lay headline but wrong if a specialist reads the pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "a region immediately in front of and above a recently identified scene-perception area (SPA) in superior parietal cortex"

*N=24 (14 female), two independent datasets, the resting-state coupling dissociation and the four-stream confluence are all accurate.*

---

### Study 17: Harder-looking Chinese characters are easier to pull out of short-term memory
**PMID:** 42612440 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Significant framing issue

**Issue A. Headline reverses the stroke-count result** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** Headline: "Harder-looking Chinese characters are easier to pull out of short-term memory"
- **Abstract says:** "accuracy for simple characters was higher than that for complex characters … simpler characters with fewer strokes are more readily retrievable from STM"
- **Problem:** "Harder-*looking*" reads as visual/graphic complexity — exactly the dimension on which the study found the *opposite* result. The counterintuitive findings concern phonetic regularity and semantic transparency, not visual complexity. The body text gets this right ("Simpler characters were retrieved more accurately, as expected"), so the headline contradicts the entry it sits above.
- **Suggested fix:** "Chinese characters that don't tell you how they sound are easier to hold in short-term memory"

*Experiments 2 and 3 (irregular > regular; non-transparent > transparent) are reported accurately, and the missing sample details are flagged.*

---

### Study 18: Targeted brain stimulation moves a network — but not the memory it was aimed at
**PMID:** 42610835 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The single-case randomised placebo-controlled design, the left cMFG target selected on peak DMN connectivity, the increase in target–DMN connectivity, the null on associative memory (primary) and the improvement in visuospatial working memory (secondary) all match. N=1 and the chance-risk of the secondary finding are properly flagged.

---

### Study 19: A nine-week course improves how older adults read between the lines
**PMID:** 42629485 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Significant framing issue

**Issue A. Omits two null/partial outcomes on targeted modalities** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Pragmatic comprehension and production improved from pre- to post-training and were maintained at three months, in both linguistic and extralinguistic channels."
- **Abstract says:** "A trend towards enhancement was also observed in paralinguistic ability, although the changes did not reach statistical significance, while no significant change emerged in sensitivity to the context."
- **Problem:** The training explicitly targeted four things — linguistic, extralinguistic, paralinguistic and context sensitivity. Two of the four did not improve significantly, including context sensitivity, which is arguably the closest thing to "reading between the lines" in the headline. Reporting only the two positives makes the intervention look broader in effect than it was.
- **Suggested fix:** "Pragmatic comprehension and production improved pre- to post-training and were maintained at three months in the linguistic and extralinguistic channels; paralinguistic gains were a non-significant trend and sensitivity to context did not change."

*N=24, ages 65–86, nine-week group format, three-month follow-up, stable cognitive/ToM measures and the authors' own "preliminary" label are all accurate. NS fit 4/10 with an explicit "no control group" caveat is appropriately conservative.*

---

### Study 20: Training working memory with emotional material curbs risky decisions
**PMID:** 42590932 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Hype in the pitch headline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Pitch angle: "Brain training's best shot yet — with an emotional twist."
- **Abstract says:** "These findings highlight eWMT as a promising cognitive-affective intervention"
- **Problem:** "Best shot yet" is a superlative comparative claim across the whole working-memory-training literature that this 30-person single-site trial cannot support — and it sits awkwardly against the digest's own line that "at this sample size it is a hypothesis, not a finding."
- **Suggested fix:** "A small trial gives working memory training an emotional twist — and a rare transfer signal"

*N=30 (15/15), 20 sessions, active feature-matching comparator, one-month follow-up, and the adaptive-strategy null are all accurate; underpowering is flagged in both the NS rationale and Caveats.*

---

### Study 21: Personalised symptom networks reveal four recurring "shapes" of PTSD
**PMID:** 42625545 → correct PMID **42607016** | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sample composition and a mislabelled model component** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Fifty-five trauma-exposed people (31 with PTSD) chose personalised items representing the components of Ehlers and Clark's cognitive model — trauma memory, triggers, negative appraisals, sense of current threat, coping strategies."
- **Abstract says:** "Fifty-five participants (31 with PTSD, 24 with clinical-level symptoms) selected personalised items reflecting core model components: negative appraisals, trauma memory, triggers, sense of current threat, and *maladaptive* strategies."
- **Problem:** Two small drifts: the comparison group is not "non-PTSD" but people with clinical-level symptoms (worth stating, as it affects how distinct the clusters can be), and "maladaptive strategies" is a specific model construct that "coping strategies" flattens.
- **Suggested fix:** "Fifty-five trauma-exposed people (31 with PTSD, 24 with clinical-level symptoms) … negative appraisals, trauma memory, triggers, sense of current threat and maladaptive strategies."

**Issue B. "Confirmed" overstates the model test** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Individual networks confirmed the model's central claim that 'sense of current threat' is the hub"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings provided empirical support for key assumptions of the E&C model, particularly the central role of sense of current threat"
- **Problem:** "Confirmed" implies a decisive test; the authors claim support for assumptions in an exploratory idiographic framework.
- **Suggested fix:** "Individual networks supported the model's central claim that 'sense of current threat' sits at the hub."

*Note: the Tim Dalgleish/MRC CBU affiliation in the pitch is unverifiable from abstract only — the PubMed record carries no affiliations. Confirm before pitching. The 41-completer EMA subsample, 2,594 observations and four subtypes are all accurate, and the exploratory status of the clusters is flagged.*

---

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Semaglutide and cognitive complaints | ⚠️ Minor issues | Omits null sitagliptin comparison; MDD subgroup framed as stronger effect rather than better powered; cohort description implies all initiated a drug |
| 2 | Sleep and source memory | ⚠️ Minor issues | Word-reduction effect was Experiment 2 only |
| 3 | Eye movements and unconscious reactivation | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline claims "therapy works" from a lab analogue, contradicting own Caveats; suggest NS 6/10 |
| 4 | 27-second false memories | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline/"Why it matters" put onset at 27 s; illusion present at zero delay |
| 5 | Enactment vs episodic future thinking | ⚠️ Minor issues | Null age interaction read as per-group effects; "age 8 to 60" unverifiable |
| 6 | Offloading vs shallow processing | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Stopping them forming" overstates a graded recall cost |
| 7 | Dual task beyond fear | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Therapy" framing for an online analogue; "Overturns prior research" overstates a null moderation |
| 8 | Off-task MTurk participants | ✅ Accurate | — |
| 9 | Offloading under overload | ⚠️ Minor issues | Load-dependence of offloading errors not stated in abstract |
| 10 | tDCS, sleep and consolidation | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Overnight" consolidation not specified in abstract |
| 11 | Enactment without vision | ⚠️ Minor issues | Overall effect + null group difference presented as effect in all three groups |
| 12 | Cheater face memory | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Most" prior studies hardened to "used the same photograph" |
| 13 | Handwriting and lexical competition | ⚠️ Minor issues | Causal headline for a predictive neural–behavioural relationship |
| 14 | CRT in schizophrenia | ✅ Accurate | — |
| 15 | Daily diaries and PTSD | ⚠️ Minor issues | Epub date given as publication date; issue is Dec 2026 |
| 16 | Fourth perception–memory pair | ⚠️ Minor issues | Localisation drops "dorsal" |
| 17 | Chinese character complexity | ⚠️ Significant framing issue | Headline reverses the stroke-count finding; body text contradicts it |
| 18 | Network moved, memory didn't | ✅ Accurate | — |
| 19 | Pragmatic training in older adults | ⚠️ Significant framing issue | Omits non-significant paralinguistic trend and null on context sensitivity |
| 20 | Emotional working memory training | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Brain training's best shot yet" unsupported superlative |
| 21 | Four shapes of PTSD | ⚠️ Minor issues | Comparison group mischaracterised; "maladaptive" → "coping" strategies; "confirmed" overstates; Dalgleish affiliation unverifiable |

**Total issues:** 24 (19 Minor, 5 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 18
**Entries cleared:** 3

**Cross-cutting note for the editor:** the most consistent pattern in this digest is a *headline* that makes a stronger or slightly different claim than the entry's own body text and Caveats — Studies 3, 4, 7, 13 and especially 17. The Caveats sections are generally strong and honest; the headlines are running ahead of them. A single pass rewriting headlines to match the body would clear most of the flagged issues. The second pattern is treating a non-significant group-by-condition interaction as evidence of an effect within every subgroup (Studies 5 and 11) — worth a standing rule.
